title: What really won the trillion-dollar Supreme Court case (TED Talk transcript)
author: Neal Kumar Katyal

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: AI advocacy: Assistance claims exceed victory evidence
st.an: Katyal supports the cluster’s augmentation framing by insisting that advocacy still required independent human judgment, but he also advances a strong victory-linked narrative through retrospective claims that Harvey predicted judicial questions and reasoning. The source provides no systematic accuracy test or causal evidence showing that those predictions determined the outcome.

kp.k: Bespoke legal AI supported Supreme Court argument preparation
kp.d: Katyal describes Harvey as a bespoke system developed with a legal-AI company over the preceding year. He says he trained it on every question asked by Supreme Court justices in the last 25 years and their written opinions. His account presents AI as an addition to an intensive legal-team preparation process, providing information processing at scale.
qs: Harvey is an AI, a bespoke system I'd been building with a legal AI company for the last year.
And I trained it on every question asked by a Supreme Court justice in the last 25 years
Harvey reads the 200th tariff case the same way as he reads  the first.

kp.k: AI reportedly anticipated judicial questions and opinion reasoning
kp.d: Katyal reports that Harvey anticipated questions about taxing power, tariffs versus embargoes, license fees and tariff refunds, as well as a possible rationale for the Chief Justice to rule in his favour. He also claims it predicted Justice Gorsuch's separate opinion almost verbatim. These are practitioner recollections from one case, rather than reported benchmark results or a systematic performance evaluation; he also describes a question Harvey did not predict.
qs: It knew that Justice Gorsuch would ask me about the taxing power.
It knew Justice Kavanaugh was going to grill me on tariffs versus embargoes.
It nailed Justice Barrett's worry about tariff refunds.
Harvey even predicted Justice Gorsuch's separate opinion  striking down the tariffs, almost verbatim.
asked the question that Harvey hadn't predicted,

kp.k: Judicial consistency makes predictive preparation possible
kp.d: Katyal argues that anticipating judicial reasoning is neither a trick nor exploitation of judicial weakness. He interprets the patterns Harvey identified as expressions of consistency and integrity, framing predictability as a desirable feature of courts.
qs: Because predictability is what we want,  especially in courts.
Predictability is just consistency made visible.
What Harvey found in these justices was not weakness.  It was integrity.

kp.k: AI should challenge lawyers rather than replace judgment
kp.d: Katyal warns that powerful tools can induce people to stop thinking and defer to computer output. He describes his team's use of Harvey as a sparring partner: AI supplied questions, while lawyers developed answers. This is an augmentation model, and his claim that simply repeating AI output would have lost the case is a rhetorical counterfactual, not a measured outcome.
qs: But if I had just parroted Harvey's output,  I would have lost the case 10-0,  and there aren't even 10 justices.
The computer says so. Four words, human judgment ends, then people just fold like a cheap lawn chair.
Harvey was not some God. It was our sparring partner, brilliant, tireless,  occasionally insufferable, but not a God.
Harvey asked the questions, we found the answer.

kp.k: AI erodes accumulated knowledge as an expert advantage
kp.d: Extending his argument beyond law, Katyal asserts that AI makes experts' traditional advantage in accumulated knowledge and pattern recognition nearly worthless because those capabilities become available to anyone. This is his broad interpretation of changing expertise, not a quantified finding about legal employment, prices or market structure.
qs: their edge was accumulated knowledge. AI is making that edge nearly worthless.
Not because  humans no longer matter, but because that particular advantage, pattern recognition across vast data  and breadth of knowledge is now available to anyone.

kp.k: Human connection becomes the advocate's distinctive contribution
kp.d: Katyal argues that persuasion through connection, responsive delivery and understanding another person's underlying concern remains irreducibly human. He attributes the decisive contribution in his argument to this capacity rather than AI prediction, illustrating it with his response to an unexpected question from Justice Barrett. His categorical claim about what AI cannot do is an advocacy thesis grounded in his personal account.
qs: AI can analyze, AI can predict,  but the one thing AI can't do  is the thing that actually won that argument, connect.
That's the last irreplaceable human skill.
Persuade one person to change their mind  by appealing to something beneath the surface.
I wanted to understand her worry.  And I answered the worry.

kp.k: Advocacy preparation combines AI with interpersonal and psychological coaching
kp.d: Katyal describes sports coaching that reframed obligation as opportunity, improvisation coaching that developed listening, and meditation coaching that supported calm. He presents these human capabilities as complements to Harvey's foresight, recommending that people deepen their distinctively human contribution rather than frame AI solely as a replacement threat.
qs: That's the essence of yes and, absorb the question and then build on it.
When the justice is attacked, I validated their concerns and then bridged back.
The interrogation became a dialogue.
Harvey gave me foresight. Liz taught me to listen.  And Bob taught me stillness.
Go deeper into it. Not to survive AI, but to come home to yourself.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Katyal claims that AI improves litigation preparation through large-scale analysis and prediction, while shifting lawyers’ distinctive contribution toward independent judgment and human connection.
pts.d: Neal Kumar Katyal describes Harvey, the legal-AI product used in a bespoke system developed with a legal-AI company, as a tireless preparation partner that identified patterns in judicial materials, anticipated questions and lines of attack, and identified a potential rationale through which the Chief Justice could support his position. He also says it predicted Justice Gorsuch’s separate opinion almost verbatim. His broader claim is that AI makes accumulated knowledge and large-scale pattern recognition widely available, substantially diminishing their value as an expert’s competitive advantage. He contrasts these capabilities with what he describes as an irreplaceably human ability to connect, listen and adapt persuasion in real time. He advocates augmentation rather than reliance on AI output alone: his team used Harvey as a sparring partner, not as an authority whose answers should simply be accepted.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered is Katyal’s first-person account of preparation for and performance in a Supreme Court tariffs case, rather than a systematic evaluation.
pts.d: Katyal grounds his claims in his experience using Harvey alongside a legal team. He reports specific predictive successes involving questions about license fees, taxing power, tariffs versus embargoes, tariff refunds, a possible route for the Chief Justice’s decision, and Justice Gorsuch’s separate opinion. He links these preparations to the six-to-three decision he describes as striking down the tariffs. He also recounts an unpredicted question from Justice Barrett, using that episode to support his argument for responsive human connection. The transcript supplies no prediction logs, accuracy denominator, benchmark, controlled comparison or independent assessment of Harvey’s contribution to the outcome. The broader claims about the declining value of knowledge-based expertise and the irreplaceability of connection are interpretive conclusions supported by his personal narrative, not separately measured findings.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The specific capability claims concern a bespoke system developed over the preceding year and used before a recent argument; the broader changes to expertise are presented as already occurring.
pts.d: Katyal places the argument five months before the talk and describes developing the bespoke Harvey system over the preceding year. He says he trained it on 25 years of Supreme Court questions and the justices’ writings, and reports a license-fee question prediction made a month before argument. These are claims about a tailored preparation system with extensive judicial material, not explicitly about any unconfigured AI product. He relates predictive usefulness to consistency in justices’ principles. He qualifies the account by acknowledging an unpredicted question and warning that powerful tools can induce people to stop thinking. His claimed successful use therefore depends on lawyers retaining independent judgment and responding to the actual exchange rather than parroting output. He offers no dated forecast for profession-wide displacement or adoption. The supplied document labels the source 2026 but ends with a conflicting event-year reference, so the relative timings are preserved rather than converted into a precise argument date.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The immediate beneficiaries described are Supreme Court advocates and litigation teams; Katyal extends the implications to knowledge-based professionals and anyone whose work requires persuasion.
pts.d: For high-stakes appellate lawyers and their teams, Katyal describes AI as expanding the scale of preparation and enabling anticipation of judicial concerns. Lawyers remain responsible for developing answers, exercising judgment and delivering persuasive responses. Judges are the subjects of the predictive analysis and the audience for advocacy, not described as being replaced by AI. More broadly, experienced lawyers and doctors are presented as losing some of the differentiation previously supplied by accumulated knowledge, while access to analytical breadth becomes more widely available. Katyal identifies listening and connection as the remaining human advantage in advocacy, interviews and negotiations. He does not make concrete claims about law-firm staffing, billing, junior-lawyer employment, client prices or access to justice.
